newsitem.title: INDONESIA: ASEAN, Australia, NZ say WTO must focus on trade.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN, Australia, NZ say WTO must focus on trade.

text.p: Trade ministers from the ASEAN group, Australia and New Zealand said on Friday they agreed the World Trade Organisation (WTO) meeting in Singapore in December should confine itself to core trade issues.
Australia's deputy prime minister and trade minister, Tim Fischer, said the WTO had been discussed in the annual talks between ASEAN, Australia and New Zealand.

"We agree with the ASEAN approach to stick to the core trade issues, and I would add particularly in relation to labour standards, which are best dealt with by the International Labour Organisation (ILO)...," Fischer told a news briefing.
"There was a great meeting of the minds on that."
Asked if New Zealand agreed with this approach, minister for trade negotiations Philip Burdon replied: "Absolutely."

ASEAN members Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, Brunei, the Philippines and Vietnam strongly oppose the introduction of what they regard as extraneous issues such as labour standards, corruption, procurement and competition policies at the WTO's inaugural ministerial meeting.
The United States and some other Western nations have said they wanted such issues raised at Singapore.

Indonesian coordinating minister of production and distribution, Hartarto, told a news conference after Friday's talks the ministers had also expressed concern at U.S. legislation "which imposes sanctions on countries or enterprises doing business with Cuba and several other countries".
This was the second annual meeting of ASEAN with Australia and New Zealand, who are linked under the Closer Economic Relations (CER) trade agreement.

The ministers said the meeting had been highly successful, and noted that two-way trade between the two regions had jumped to $15.8 billion in 1995 from $7.9 billion in 1990, and that ASEAN accounted for 14 percent of Australian-New Zealand exports.
They said cooperation was progressing well and they were looking for further ways to enhance trade and investment, and in particular to ensure the participation of the private sector.
Hartarto said the meeting called on the business community to identify constraints which might hinder investment and trade.

The two sides signed a framework memorandum of understanding for cooperation on standards and conformance between the two regions -- the first such accord signed by either side with another trading region.
The memorandum covered such areas as weights and measures, documentary standards and accreditation of testing, inspection and certification bodies.
The meeting followed two days of talks among the ASEAN ministers on progress in implementing the ASEAN free trade area (AFTA) and other economic issues.
